The upcoming MacBook Ultra is definitely not going to come cheap. Beyond its all-new, slimmer design, OLED display, and touch functionality, there's also the added pricing pressure from rising memory costs. The latest report suggests that production costs could be pushed even higher.

Apple has always preferred to source components from multiple suppliers to improve display stability and secure the best pricing leverage. The company originally hoped to adopt the same strategy for the MacBook Ultra. However, supply chain sources indicate that Apple has decided to use only a single display supplier...

Apple has three display partners in its product lineup: Samsung, LG, and BOE. BOE currently only supplies displays for the company's lower-end products, while orders for high-end displays are split between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature the most sophisticated display ever on an Apple product. Combining stacked OLED with touch functionality on the large-size panels required for laptops is no easy feat. The latest supply chain report reveals that Apple has decided to source these displays exclusively from Samsung.

According to The Elec, LG was unable to meet the production volumes required by Apple.

Apple asked its partners to respond with large-size substrates for mass production. Samsung Display responded with its 8.6-generation OLED production line, while LG Display is reportedly studying the continued use of its existing 6-generation production line. Although the 6-generation line can produce OLED panels for laptops, its substrate efficiency and capacity fall short of the 8.6-generation line. Due to early yield shortfalls, Apple ultimately chose Samsung Display as its sole supplier.

It seems the small-scale volume LG can produce isn't worth the additional logistical complexity of maintaining two suppliers. LG is not expected to manufacture displays for this flagship MacBook before 2029.

This situation clearly puts Samsung in a stronger position in panel price negotiations, which could further drive up Apple's production costs—and Apple is expected to pass these costs on to consumers, just as it has done with rising memory costs.

The MacBook Ultra's price tag could be eye-wateringly expensive. How interested are you in considering an upgrade? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
